title: The 25 Sheriff and Prosecutor Races Set to Shape Criminal Justice and ICE Collaboration
author: Daniel Nichanian
content:
When Danny Tarkenton learned that federal agents had shot and killed Renee
Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis last winter, she felt concerned that her
local officials would not push back should similar violence unfold in her own
backyard in Spokane, Washington. “That’s why I ran to protect my community,”
she told _Bolts_. “We can sue the agents under state crimes.”

Tarkenton is now running for chief prosecutor of Spokane County, challenging a
Republican incumbent who opposes his state’s sanctuary protections. She is
among the many candidates for prosecutor or sheriff this fall who say they got
in to push back against President Trump’s mass deportations agenda. The
challenger to an upstate New York sheriff says he wants to “kick ICE out”; in
North Carolina, another challenger is accusing the sheriff’s office of racial
profiling.

But even as immigration has electrified prosecutor and sheriff races during
the midterms, many other decisions await November’s winners. These are
offices, after all, with vast powers over policing and punishment.

All in all, there are [2,400 contests](https://boltsmag.org/whats-on-the-
ballot/prosecutor-and-sheriff-elections-in-2026/) for sheriff and prosecutor
this year, and though many drew just one candidate, plenty offer voters stark
choices on the criminal legal system.

Police misconduct looms large over November’s sheriff elections in
Springfield, Illinois, and Tacoma, Washington. In Los Angeles, Minneapolis,
and Omaha, voters face critical choices over how punitive prosecutors should
be. And in Fort Worth, where the district attorney’s office has used its power
to aggressively police elections, candidates are signaling they’d take
opposite approaches to voting cases like the one of Crystal Mason, a woman who
was sentenced to years in prison for mistakenly thinking she could vote while
she was on probation.

_Bolts_ has reported on some of the nation’s [most
pivotal](https://boltsmag.org/buncombe-county-district-attorney-sheriff-
elections-and-state-preemption/) [contests](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-
county-sheriff-terry-johnson-shannon-long/) [all
year](https://boltsmag.org/with-latest-win-progressive-vermont-prosecutor-
looks-to-double-down-on-reforms/). Today, we identify the 25 elections you
should monitor most closely heading into November.

### **California | Los Angeles County sheriff**

Alex Villanueva is mounting yet another comeback. Four years after he was
handily ousted as sheriff by Robert Luna, Villanueva qualified for the
November runoff by finishing second in the June primary, behind Luna. He only
received 22 percent of the vote.

The race is nonpartisan but Luna is a Democrat and Villanueva is now a
Republican.

Villanueva’s tenure was marred by serial scandals and investigations into
abuses and organized violence among deputies, as _Bolts_
[reported](https://boltsmag.org/unease-in-los-angeles-sheriff-race/) in 2022
during Luna and Villanueva’s first electoral showdown.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Villanueva.jpg)Alex
Villanueva, the sheriff of Los Angeles (Los Angeles Sheriff's
Department/Facebook)

Scandals at the sheriff’s office have persisted under Luna; for instance, jail
deaths [keep](https://boltsmag.org/los-angeles-county-board-of-supervisors-
alex-villanueva-jail-deaths/) [mounting](https://www.vera.org/news/la-county-
jail-deaths), and Luna has refused to comply with
[subpoenas](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-03-20/los-angeles-
sheriff-sues-oversight-commission) from an oversight body investigating
controversial cases in which deputies beat or shot people. In 2022, and again
this spring, progressives who hoped to reform the office [rallied
around](https://boltsmag.org/unease-in-los-angeles-sheriff-race/) another
candidate, Eric Strong, but he finished third in both cycles and did not
advance to the general election.

### **California | Los Angeles city attorney**

City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto had a rocky tenure, including facing
backlash for trying to[ lift](https://lapublicpress.org/2025/10/no-kings-
rally-press-protections/) restrictions on the LAPD using force against
journalists; then she lost her reelection bid as early as the June primary,
finishing third behind Marissa Roy, who ran to her left, and John McKinney,
who ran to the right.

Now, the November faceoff between McKinney and Roy is pitting drastically
different visions of the office against one another. Roy says she’ll do more
to flex the powers of the office to protect tenants and hold police
accountable; McKinney has emphasized prosecuting misdemeanors to combat crime
and homelessness, building on messaging that led Nathan Hochman to win the
county’s DA race two years ago. Stay tuned for more in _Bolts_.

### **Illinois | Sangamon County sheriff**

After a Sangamon County sheriff’s deputy shot and killed Sonya Massey in 2024,
sparking nationwide protest and the resignation of the local sheriff, a
citizen commission met for over a year to discuss how to prevent future
tragedies, [_Bolts_ reported last year](https://boltsmag.org/sonya-massey-
commission-springfield-illinois-police-reform/). The panel released a final
report in late 2025 that recommended dozens of reforms to transform policing
and mental health services in the county, for instance dispatching civilian
teams to respond to some emergency calls.

Now, voters this fall are electing their sheriff, who will be in charge of
actually implementing many of these changes. Republican Paula Crouch, who was
appointed sheriff by county officials after Massey’s murder, faces Democratic
challenger Marc Bell.

Bell told _Bolts_ that __ he was impressed by the Massey Commission and
“looked forward to moving some of their suggestions forward,” though he did
not name a particular policy he wanted to implement when asked for specifics.
To a follow-up query about whether he’d favor setting up a civilian panel with
power to subpoena the sheriff’s office, a key demand of the commission, he
said he “wouldn’t have a problem with it”; Bell currently sits on a police
that is tasked with oversight over Springfield’s municipal police but lacks
the power to actually investigate misconduct.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/12/571121920_122147706902649977_5905482618883099483_n.jpg)The
Massey Commission during its final meeting and ratification session on Oct.
27, 2025. (Facebook/Massey Commission)

Sunshine Clemons, a member of the Massey Commission and co-founder of the
Springfield Black Lives Matter chapter, told _Bolts_ that local officials,
including the appointed sheriff, have shared verbal support for the calls to
action, but that there’s been little by way of concrete changes over the last
year. Crouch’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

“What I’m looking for in our next sheriff is someone who doesn’t just say,
‘Yes, these are important,’ but actually has a strategic plan to implement
these calls to action,” Clemons told _Bolts_. “We’re well past the time of
words and platitude.” She hopes the sheriff’s office starts releasing ongoing
updates about how they’re actually acting on last year’s recommendations. In
the meantime, she and other former members of the Massey Commission
[launched](https://capitolcitynow.com/news/248842-from-massey-commission-to-
massey-community-action-network-how-community-and-family-want-to-keep-sonyas-
name-alive/) a new coalition this summer that they hope can continue to
pressure the county to make reforms.

### **Louisiana | Prosecutors in East Baton Rouge Parish, and in Morehouse and Ouachita parishes**

Ryan Thompson, a prominent defense attorney in East Baton Rouge, Louisiana’s
largest parish, has clashed with the local justice system over the years. He
was a lead attorney in [federal civil rights
lawsuits](https://www.wbrz.com/news/brave-cave-fallout-still-happening-
lawsuits-stacking-up) against the Baton Rouge Police Department over
allegations that officers [routinely abused
people](https://www.wafb.com/2023/11/14/i-team-new-brave-cave-lawsuit-alleges-
man-faced-humiliating-strip-search) during interrogations inside a nearly
empty police warehouse, and he has
[denounced](https://www.wbrz.com/videos/murder-suspect-accidentally-let-out-
of-jail-turns-himself-in-hours-later) local law enforcement for “differential
treatment between Black and white defendants.”

Now he is challenging DA Hillar Moore, making this the incumbent’s first
contested race since 2008.

Moore last year [supported](https://www.wafb.com/2024/11/22/court-experts-
opposite-sides-weigh-proposed-constitutional-amendment-juvenile-crime/) a
[constitutional amendment championed by Louisiana
Republicans](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-amendment-3-youth-prosecution-
adult-system/) that would have made it easier to prosecute children as adults,
a proposal that Louisianans ended up rejecting by a huge margin. He has also
[resisted efforts](https://boltsmag.org/the-death-penalty-on-trial-in-
louisiana/) for clemency for people on death row. Now, Moore and a political
committee that supports him are targeting Thompson’s job as a defense attorney
by attacking his [work on behalf of
people](https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/courts/district-attorney-
hillar-moore-ryan-thompson/article_d9c2e41b-5a45-428d-9121-ac1e75e47729.html)
accused of violence offenses.

_Bolts_ is also watching Louisiana’s 4th District, home to Morehouse and
Ouachita parishes.

DA Steven Tew is currently overseeing the continued efforts to prosecute Jimmy
Duncan, a man who spent 26 years on death row [until his conviction was
overturned last year](https://boltsmag.org/chris-duncan-louisiana-death-row-
conviction-set-aside/). _Bolts_ [has reported extensively on the discredited
evidence](https://boltsmag.org/the-human-cost-of-jeff-landrys-drive-to-resume-
executions/) in the case, and how the prosecution relied on two forensic
experts peddling junk science who have been responsible for many wrongful
convictions.

Tew is retiring this year, and the election to replace him may shape Duncan’s
case. Stay tuned for more in _Bolts_.

### **Maine | Cumberland County (Portland) prosecutor**

When she ousted DA Jonathan Sahrbeck four years ago, Democrat Jackie Sartoris
claimed the mantle of reform and [told
_Bolts_](https://boltsmag.org/cumberland-county-prosecutor-election/) she
wished to scale back how often prosecutors seek prison sentences for lower-
level offenses. In office, Sartoris rolled out some changes, like [no longer
prosecuting](https://wgme.com/news/local/maine-da-wont-charge-unlicensed-
drivers-to-focus-on-more-serious-cases-cumberland-county-district-attorney-
jacqueline-sartoris-prosecutor) cases of driving with a suspended license and
[expanding](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/04/cumberland-county-da-
jackie-sartoris-announces-reelection-campaign) [diversion
programs](https://www.mainepublic.org/courts-and-crime/2026-04-06/cumberland-
county-da-expands-restorative-justice-program-to-offer-defendants-way-to-
avoid-conviction) to help defendants avoid a record over low-level offenses.

These policies are squarely in the mold of what reform DAs across the country
have pursued, but, in a [common pattern](https://boltsmag.org/vermont-reform-
prosecutor-wins-after-police-union-attacks/) nationwide, they’ve drawn
hostility from local police unions.

This fall, police are [backing her
challenger](https://www.newscentermaine.com/article/news/politics/maine-
politics/cumberland-county-da-jackie-sartoris-portland-police-unions-
endorsement/97-053f3cc9-1e50-4c9c-a092-cbba348185bd), Stephanie Anderson, who
held the office from 1991 to 2018 as a Republican and is now mounting a
comeback as an independent. Anderson has attacked Sartoris’ approach as
endangering public safety, while the incumbent has defended her changes as
“long overdue progressive reforms,” [_The Press Herald_
reports](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/07/16/former-longtime-cumberland-
county-district-attorney-affirms-candidacy/).

### **Maryland | Frederick County and Wicomico County sheriffs**

Chuck Jenkins, the 20-year sheriff of Maryland’s Frederick County, 50 miles
from the nation's capital, has made his office a force multiplier for ICE long
before the Trump administration, and long before it was commonplace among
sheriffs, [_Bolts_ reported last week](https://boltsmag.org/frederick-county-
immigration-enforcement-sheriff-chuck-jenkins/).

“The fear and the justified state of terror and hysteria that folks have been
put in nationally under this administration is what folks have been living
under in Frederick for years,” Sebastian Brown, a Frederick resident and
advocate at the ACLU of Maryland, told _Bolts_. “That fear has been here since
2008 and permeated every part of people’s lives.”

Jenkins, a Republican, is now running for a sixth term against Democrat Karl
Bickel, a former sheriff's deputy who has lost to Jenkins by tightening
margins in each of the last three cycles; Jenkins prevailed by just 3
percentage points four years ago. Bickel and Jenkins appear to viscerally
detest each other. “I’d kick his ass, personally. Physically. I’d stomp his
ass,” Jenkins told a _Bolts_ reporter.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/IMG_8425-2400x1800.jpg)Frederick County Sheriff Chuck
Jenkins is running for a sixth term. (Photo by Alex Burness for _Bolts_)

On the other side of Maryland, another longtime sheriff
[affiliated](https://www.delmarvanow.com/story/news/local/maryland/2025/12/02/wicomicos-
mike-lewis-named-as-sheriff-of-year-by-conservative-group/87552103007/?gnt-
cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-
epti=z113109p001550c001550e007700v113109&gca-ft=104&gca-ds=sophi) with
national right-wing groups is also seeking reelection. In red-leaning Wicomico
County, Sheriff Mike Lewis made a name for himself last decade in conservative
circuits [by proclaiming](https://marylandreporter.com/2014/08/20/gun-wars-
wicomico-co-sheriff-among-many-who-wont-enforce-some-gun-bans/) his county is
a “Second Amendment sanctuary” and refusing to enforce state gun control laws.

He called Maryland a “Disneyland for illegal immigrants” at a public meeting
last year, in which he and other county officials decided to bow to state
pressure and table their hopes of joining ICE’s 287(g) program—a partnership
that effectively empowers some local deputies to act as federal immigration
agents.

He faces Democratic challenger Lana Foley, who worked with protesters last
year in advocating against partnering with ICE, [saying at a public
meeting](https://www.wboc.com/news/potential-agreement-between-wicomico-
county-and-ice-continues-to-receive-
backlash/article_1a2dcbf8-4867-40de-8ca0-804a7bd69856.html), “The 287(g)
program isn’t about safety, it’s about fear and control.” She later
[urged](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/cmte_testimony/2026/jpr/32449_02032026_11243-894.pdf)
lawmakers to ban the program—which they ultimately did with a [law passed
early this year](https://boltsmag.org/maryland-new-mexico-ban-local-contracts-
with-ice/).

### **Minnesota | Hennepin County (Minneapolis) prosecutor**

Four years after her [victory in
Minneapolis](https://boltsmag.org/minneapolis-public-defender-turned-
prosecutor/) made her one of the most visible members of the progressive
prosecutor movement, Mary Moriarty chose to not seek reelection this year.

During her sole term, the career public defender worked to dial back
sentencing for some offenses, [clashing](https://boltsmag.org/minnesotas-
keith-ellison-thwarts-a-reform-prosecutor-he-endorsed/) with some of her
party’s officials in the process. And this year she has sought to [flex her
authority](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/27/us/prosecutors-charges-against-
federal-agents.html) to prosecute ICE agents for violent acts, though her
efforts have run into the Trump administration’s stonewalling.

Two candidates are facing off to replace her and, [much like in the 2022
election](https://boltsmag.org/election-for-hennepin-county-attorney-
minneapolis/), they have support from opposite factions who disagree on the
best path to safety for Minneapolis. State Representative Cederick Frazier,
himself a [former public
defender](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/08/20/cedrick-frazier-hennepin-
county-attorney-race), is [more aligned](https://www.startribune.com/hennepin-
county-attorney-race-cedrick-frazier-dfl-endorsement/601856726) with Moriarty;
he has endorsements from progressive officials, including U.S. Representative
Ilhan Omar as well as Moriarty allies and prominent reform prosecutors
Philadelphia DA Larry Krasner and Travis County (Austin) DA Jose Garza,.

Frazier faces Anders Folk, a longtime prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney’s
Office, who promises a break from Moriarty’s approach to the office. “Day one,
for me, the Mary Moriarty era ends,” he has said, [making the
case](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/08/19/hennepin-county-attorney-race-
narrows-down-to-anders-folk-and-cedrick-frazier) that she is not punitive
enough toward people with repeat offenses. He has the support from Jacob Frey,
the city’s centrist mayor, and city council members who have aligned with the
mayor [on law enforcement](https://boltsmag.org/minneapolis-policing-
and-2025-elections/) matters.

### **  
Montana | Gallatin County (Bozeman) prosecutor and sheriff**

Angered by local immigration raids, frustrated by the Gallatin County
sheriff’s partnership with ICE, and then dispirited that said
sheriff—Republican Dan Springer—drew no challenger this year for the second
consecutive cycle, Bozeman activist Garrett Grim decided to launch a write-in
campaign for sheriff this year.

“I wanted to run so that I could protect the rights of all residents in
Gallatin County and be able to establish a county sheriff that was responsive
to the people,” Grimm told _Bolts._ “I do not like bullies. I believe that
they need to be stood up to.”

Even if his odds of winning are low, Grimm says he hopes that his campaign can
build more awareness of Springer’s record of partnering with ICE, which is
unusual for a public official in a swing county that voted for Kamala Harris
over Trump. In fact, such activism and [months of
protests](https://montanafreepress.org/2026/01/26/montanans-turn-out-en-masse-
to-protest-ice-killings/) already spurred the county commission to [step in
this summer](https://www.explorebigsky.com/gallatin-county-commissioners-end-
disputed-287g-agreement-after-public-outreach/171699) to end Springer’s
contract with the federal agency.

Immigrants’ rights also loom large in the county’s prosecutor race, where
Democratic County Attorney Audrey Cromwell is running for reelection.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/471678272_579139088050710_3642986478508727778_n.jpg)Audrey
Cromwell is running for reelection in Gallatin County, one of Montana’s most
politically competive counties (photo via County Attorney Audrey
Cromwell/Facebook)

Cromwell has faced attacks over the last year from Montana Attorney General
Austin Knusden, a Republican who said she is violating state law by refusing
to [share information with
ICE](https://montanafreepress.org/2026/04/02/montana-attorney-general-accuses-
gallatin-county-of-not-sharing-information-with-ice/) and has claimed the
authority to [supervise her office](https://www.kbzk.com/news/montana-
news/gallatin-county-attorney-asks-montana-supreme-court-to-rule-on-knudsen-
takeover). Cromwell [asked state courts](https://www.kbzk.com/news/montana-
news/gallatin-county-attorney-asks-montana-supreme-court-to-rule-on-knudsen-
takeover) to shield her from Knusden but [she is still waiting for a
ruling](https://montanafreepress.org/2026/09/08/audrey-cromwell-austin-
knudsen/).

Cromwell’s GOP opponent this fall, Jordan Salo, is [mirroring Knusden’s
attacks](https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=pfbid021xyqgzQvmtDxwHHo2srrD5ZjSRAvbi3hH4nmxxq6ifhp8XZMS3a7F4UXCi7avZ2Bl&id=61588518433626);
her campaign did not reply to a request for comment on how she’d assist ICE.

Cromwell has faced attacks over the last year from Montana Attorney General
Austin Knusden, a Republican who said she is violating state law by refusing
to [share information with
ICE](https://montanafreepress.org/2026/04/02/montana-attorney-general-accuses-
gallatin-county-of-not-sharing-information-with-ice/) and has claimed the
authority to [supervise her office](https://www.kbzk.com/news/montana-
news/gallatin-county-attorney-asks-montana-supreme-court-to-rule-on-knudsen-
takeover). Cromwell [asked state courts](https://www.kbzk.com/news/montana-
news/gallatin-county-attorney-asks-montana-supreme-court-to-rule-on-knudsen-
takeover) to shield her from Knusden but [she is still waiting for a
ruling](https://montanafreepress.org/2026/09/08/audrey-cromwell-austin-
knudsen/).

Cromwell’s GOP opponent this fall, Jordan Salo, is [mirroring Knusden’s
attacks](https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=pfbid021xyqgzQvmtDxwHHo2srrD5ZjSRAvbi3hH4nmxxq6ifhp8XZMS3a7F4UXCi7avZ2Bl&id=61588518433626);
her campaign did not reply to a request for comment on how she’d assist ICE.

### **  
****Nebraska | Douglas County (Omaha) prosecutor and sheriff  **

During the 2020 Black Lives Matter movement, the Nebraska Democratic Party
condemned Doug Kleine, DA of Douglas County (Omaha), for failing to press
charges against a white bar owner who killed a Black protester. Kleine
responded by becoming a Republican.

Even before his party switch, Kleine was pursuing punitive policies, as
[_Bolts_ reported during his last reelection](https://boltsmag.org/omaha-
prosecutor-race-nebraska-prisons/) including opposing criminal justice reforms
and seeking frequent death sentences. He has maintained that approach since
then. Last year, Kaine [was a big
champion](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/08/25/pillen-kleine-highlight-
lb-530-changes-defend-detaining-teens-as-young-as-11/) of a legislative
package that made an [array of
changes](https://www.wowt.com/2025/08/25/nebraska-gov-pillen-signs-juvenile-
justice-reform-bill-into-law/) to increase criminal penalties.

One of the law’s most debated aspects was that it lowered the minimum age of
detention to 11.

Omaha’s GOP sheriff, Aaron Hanson, joined Kleine in championing the law and
defending more punitive practices toward teenage defendants. Hanson has also
tried to convince county officials to cooperate more closely with ICE, though
his push to transform the local jail into an immigrant detention center [has
been rebuffed so far](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/10/10/sheriff-
proposal-to-lease-douglas-county-jail-space-to-feds-for-migrant-detainees-
appears-iced-out/).

Kleine and Hanson now face Democrats in this competitive county. Kleine’s
challenger is Makayla Danner, an Omaha city prosecutor who [criticized the
2025 law](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2025/08/30/makayla-danner-longtime-
omaha-prosecutor-seeks-douglas-county-attorney-post/) as she launched her
campaign. Hanson’s challenger, Mark Martinez, did not reply to a request for
comment on his views. Martinez faced a contentious road to the ballot as a
local election official briefly said he was ineligible to run until the state
supreme court [reversed that
decision](https://nebraskaexaminer.com/2026/03/18/nebraska-supreme-court-
justice-puts-mark-martinez-back-on-ballot-for-douglas-county-sheriff/).

### **New York | Broome County, Orange County, and Otsego County sheriffs**

Fred Akshar, the Republican sheriff of Broome County, [testified in
Congress](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/broome-sheriff-defends-
ice-lawsuit-194537206.html) in September against New York Democrats’ efforts
to restrict partnerships with ICE. His county voted for Harris over Trump two
years ago, but that didn’t stop Ashkar from embracing the president’s
deportation agenda and joining ICE’s 287(g) program. He has remained defiant
since the state passed a law this spring banning some forms of local
cooperation with ICE, joining a lawsuit to block the law [alongside 14 other
New York sheriffs](https://www.timesunion.com/capitol/article/law-banning-ice-
agreements-scuttle-federal-22404133.php).

Akshar faces Democrat Matt Ryan, a former Binghamton mayor who is running on a
drastically different approach and [says he wants
to](https://www.facebook.com/permalink.php?story_fbid=pfbid02kyZXCDBmJtcESFwCP19Xv1cNp3NmCJnCVgsAa28DMVHjNtVRLPpTL3oBUxL7ak4bl&id=100094257750231)
“kick ICE out.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/24079535131112-scaled.jpg)Broome County Sheriff Fred
Ashkar, here shown at the u.S. Capitol with U.S. Rep. Marc Molinaro in March
2024, testified this fall in Congress against immigrant protections. (Tom
Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images)

Ryan, who unsuccessfully ran for DA in 2023, was arrested alongside other
protesters that year during a local gathering to commemorate the murder of
Tyre Nichols by Tennessee police. “We all know that they police certain
communities and treat certain communities differently,” [Ryan told _Bolts_ at
the time](https://boltsmag.org/new-york-district-attorney-sheriff-
elections-2023/). “If you’re not in a position of power to change it, then
it’s not going to change.”

Several other New York sheriffs who have assisted ICE are also running for
reelection. Otsego County Sheriff Richard Devlin actually lost the GOP primary
in June to challenger Michael Stalter, who said he wanted to quit the 287(g)
program that Devlin joined—an unusual campaign plank in a GOP primary. But
Devlin remains on the ballot as the Conservative Party nominee.

In populous Orange County, 60 miles north of New York City, Republican Sheriff
Paul Arteta has joined the lawsuit against the restrictions on ICE
collaboration, a move [condemned
by](https://www.facebook.com/BernieRiversforSheriff/posts/for-immediate-
releaseorange-county-sheriff-candidate-bernie-riverscriticizes-
she/1072151678534135/) his Democratic challenger Bernie Rivers. Arteta had
rented out space in his local jail for ICE to detain immigrants, an
arrangement [he had to end in August](https://www.thephoto-
news.com/news/local-news/orange-county-correctional-facility-ends-contract-
with-ice-NC6163582) due to the new law.

None of the other New York sheriffs who joined the pro-ICE lawsuit, or signed
a 287(g) contract, face a contested race this fall, according to _Bolts’_
analysis. A few are on the ballot this year and face no opponent; but most of
these sheriffs are not up for reelection until 2027 or 2028.

### **  
****North Carolina | Alamance County sheriff**

Sheriff Terry Johnson has faced accusations of racism and illegal policing
throughout his lengthy tenure. The DOJ investigated him over a decade ago for
fostering “a culture of discrimination against Latinos,” and immigrants’
rights protests have continued as Johnson has on-and-off partnered with ICE.

_Bolts_ and _NC Local_ [reported earlier this year on the climate of fear in
the county](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-
shannon-long/). Johnson, a Republican, faces independent challenger Shannon
Long, who says he wants to rebuild trust with local immigrant communities.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/20260510_ALAMANCE_BOLTS_042-e1781624929392.jpg)Shannon
Long, a pastor vying for sheriff in Alamance County, talks to a voter on May
9, 2026. (Photo by Jacob Biba for _Bolts_)

Long is making the case that immigration enforcement should primarily be a
federal responsibility. “We’re going to do our job, and our job is not to do
what they’re doing, which is, right now, racial profiling,” he said.

### **  
****North Carolina | Forsyth County (Winston-Salem) prosecutor**

Forsyth County DA Jim O’Neill has been a highly visible
[opponent](https://journalnow.com/nc-bills-would-legalize-possessing-up-
to-4-ounces-of-marijuana-for-personal-
use/article_7649b9d2-2d26-551c-8940-fa3d5f62354a.html) of criminal justice
reforms in North Carolina—a posture that has matched the punitive practices
he’s pursued in the DA’s office. _Carolina Public Press_ [reported in
2023](https://carolinapublicpress.org/60050/stacked-against-when-prosecutors-
stack-charges-against-a-defendant-it-can-mean-a-lifetime-behind-bars/), for
instance, on how O’Neill’s staff stacks charges against defendants to obtain
life sentences. O’Neill even [called
on](https://www.theassemblync.com/news/politics/innocence-commission-state-
budget-new-name/) the legislature to target the state’s Innocence Inquiry
Commission when it found evidence that people convicted in his county may be
innocent.

O’Neill stands out as a GOP official in a county that voted against Trump in
each of the last three presidential elections. In fact, O’Neill himself lost
his home county by 12 points in 2020 when he ran for North Carolina attorney
general; he narrowly lost statewide to Democrat Josh Stein, who has since
become the governor.

But he has faced little opposition when he has run locally. He ran unopposed
in 2010 to first secure the office, and was unopposed again in 2014 and 2018.
But then he only narrowly prevailed when he faced a challenger in
[2022](https://boltsmag.org/prosecutor-and-sheriff-elections-november-2022/).
This year, his Democratic challenger is Amara Hunter, a former prosecutor who
now works as a public defender. Hunter’s campaign declined interview requests
about her platform unless supplied with advance questions, which _Bolts_
declined; she has [said elsewhere](https://wfuogb.com/29081/city-state/local-
candidates-speak-at-wake-forest-college-democrats-forum/) she wants to lessen
the burdens of low-level convictions.

### **Texas | Tarrant County County and Fort Bend County prosecutors**   

Long before Trump began sowing unfounded doubts about the 2020 presidential
race, Republicans in Tarrant County, home to Fort Worth, were notorious for
their [selective enforcement of election laws](https://theappeal.org/texas-da-
who-sent-woman-to-prison-for-five-years-for-voting-made-her-own-election-
mistake/) and for the harsh [prosecution of Crystal
Mason](https://www.texasobserver.org/the-casualties-of-texas-war-on-voter-
fraud/), a woman who mistakenly thought she could vote while on probation and
was sentenced years in prison.

DA Phil Sorrells, who came into office after the 2022 midterms, has continued
that legacy. He [helped launch](https://boltsmag.org/tarrant-county-election-
fraud-task-force/) a task force to police local elections, and he [continued
to prosecute](https://www.texastribune.org/2024/04/25/crystal-mason-illegal-
voting-texas-tarrant-county/) Mason even after an appeals court overturned her
conviction [in 2024](https://www.texastribune.org/2024/03/28/texas-illegal-
voting-conviction-crystal-mason/). This fall, he filed [criminal
charges](https://fortworthreport.org/2026/09/10/former-legislator-seeks-
tarrant-county-judges-removal-for-official-misconduct/) against Lon Burnam, a
former state lawmaker who was expelled from a public meeting and forcibly
arrested for speaking out against a GOP plan to dramatically reduce polling
places.

Sorrells faces Democratic challenger Tiffany Burks in a competitive rematch of
their [2022 election](https://boltsmag.org/the-culture-warrior-prosecutor/).
Burks, who has worked as a prosecutor in the office, has signaled a very
different direction from Sorrells on such cases. “We are talking about a
county where they are doing everything that they can to suppress the vote,”
she said[ in an interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0iuAZ3EGK00) last
month.

She is currently [representing](https://fortworthreport.org/2026/09/10/former-
legislator-seeks-tarrant-county-judges-removal-for-official-misconduct/)
Burnam in court, and she said [last
month](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0iuAZ3EGK00) that her “first item on
business” as DA would be to drop the county’s efforts to reinstate Mason’s
conviction. (That won’t be necessary after all: Texas' highest criminal court
ruled in favor of Mason and against Sorrells on Sept. 24,[ upholding Mason’s
2024 acquittal](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/24/texas-court-
crystal-mason-voting-case).)

_The Guardian_[reported](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2026/sep/24/texas-court-crystal-mason-voting-case) this week that
Sorrells’ wife knocked on Mason's door and asked her to support her
husband—despite the DA's ongoing prosecution of Mason.

Fort Bend County, in the Houston region, is also hosting a DA race that may be
competitive.

Here, Democratic DA Brian Middleton faces Republican Shawn McDonald, who is
making the case that the office should be more punitive than under Middleton,
and who claims that the incumbent has pursued a liberal agenda in refusing to
prosecute some crimes. McDonald’s campaign did not respond to _Bolts_ ’ __
inquiry for more information. Middleton signed statements earlier this decade
saying he [would not prosecute](https://www.texastribune.org/2022/09/24/texas-
prosecutors-abortion-restrictions) abortion cases and [rebuffing Attorney
General Ken Paxton’s directive](https://abcnews.com/Politics/texas-district-
attorneys-push-back-gov-abbotts-child/story) to investigate gender-affirming
care as “child abuse.”

### **  
****Washington | Klickitat County and Pierce County sheriffs**

A ballot measure in Pierce County, Washington’s second largest county and home
to Tacoma, would end sheriff elections altogether, [_Bolts_
reports](https://boltsmag.org/pierce-county-sheriff-elections-or-
appointments/).

It would also cut short the term of Keith Swank, the right-wing sheriff who
has trumpeted his opposition to the state’s immigrant protections ever since
he won this office in 2024. In testifying against the measure in front of a
county board earlier this year, Swank also said he is proud that he is the
sheriff facing the most open complaints for misconduct at a state oversight
agency.

Should [the measure](https://boltsmag.org/pierce-county-sheriff-elections-or-
appointments/) pass, the Democratic executive would appoint a new sheriff in
early 2027.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/PierceCounty-e1787273039403.jpg)Voters in Pierce
County, Washington, will decide whether to cut the term of their sheriff short
(photo via Pierce County sheriff/Facebook).

On the other side of Washington, Klichitat County Sheriff Bob Songer, another
prominent far-right sheriff, is retiring this year, and voters will decide
whether to maintain or change the direction of the office. Songer, part of the
[“constitutional sheriffs” movement](https://www.investigatewest.org/in-a-
rural-stretch-of-washington-a-constitutional-sheriff-and-his-growing-
volunteer-posse-provoke-controversy/) that claims sheriffs have ultimate
authority to enforce the U.S. Constitution, has
[refused](https://www.newyorker.com/news/us-journal/a-coronavirus-turf-war-in-
klickitat-county) to [apply state
laws](https://q13fox.com/2019/01/29/klickitat-county-sheriff-wont-enforce-new-
washington-gun-laws/) and [he has
said](https://www.opb.org/article/2023/03/06/klickitat-washington-sheriff-bob-
songer-loren-culp-politics-jail-administrator/) he derives authority from the
“Supreme Judge of the Universe.”

Two candidates are facing off to replace him: Tony Warren, a Republican who
says [he agrees with Songer’s
approach](https://www.columbiagorgenews.com/news/tony-warrens-tenure-at-the-
bingen-white-salmon-police-
department/article_3aadf406-29b9-49d2-ba26-7659a4898eb3.html?fbclid=IwY2xjawUc5QRwZG9mAWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMTlzbjh4b2M1NFFtdU1rdnBzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEeX3bHzTRVMWypjhjSwm8ioavQasXyOj3cSH9f20A0ICW_mGci4ojqWcxan08_aem_DjEAEgq_hbdECPn7qvumqw),
including that the sheriff has the power to reject state laws, versus
independent candidate Dwayne Matulovich, who has said he [disagrees with those
views](https://skamania-dispatch.ghost.io/your-klickitat-2026-primary-ballot-
preview-7-9-7-14-candidate-forums/).

### **Washington | Spokane County prosecutor**

Larry Haskell, Spokane’s GOP prosecutor from 2014 until his premature
resignation in 2025, brought a punitive approach to the office. The
[_Spokesman-Review_](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2019/may/19/as-
counties-around-the-state-move-to-reduce-felony) reported in 2019 that Spokane
County was prosecuting far more cases at the felony level, which triggers the
harshest sentences, than other large Washington counties, a finding confirmed
by a [review of county
practices](https://www.spokanecounty.gov/DocumentCenter/View/35530/Blueprint-
for-Reform-Status-Update-October-2020) later published by local
[officials](https://www.spokanecounty.gov/875/Council). Haskell also used his
discretion to try to [circumvent sentencing
reforms](https://www.huffpost.com/entry/thomas-butler-spokane-county-three-
strikes-larry-haskell_n_62a90272e4b0c77098a6ebc2). Haskell was replaced in
mid-2025 by Preston McCollam, his chief criminal deputy, who is now running
for a full term as a Republican.

McCollam’s record is unsurprisingly entangled with that of his former boss. He
followed Haskell’s lead [in
2023](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2023/sep/03/prosecutor-asks-judge-to-
recuse-himself-in-spokane/) to argue that a local judge should not hear
criminal cases because he criticized racism in Spokane County, for instance.
As prosecutor, he has mirrored other Republicans in denouncing Washington’s
restrictions on local law enforcement collaborating with ICE,
[saying](https://www.khq.com/news/wa-law-insulates-undocumented-immigrants-
accused-of-violent-crimes-from-prosecution-says-law-
enforcement/article_cf277f2a-1bb4-45a0-9f13-aebb6049c45e.html) they are
“insulating criminal actors.” (McCollam’s campaign did not reply to requests
for an interview.)

McCollam faces Tarkenton, who is challenging him as an independent and has
support from local Democrats, including Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown. Tarkenton
says she thinks the office is too focused on the tools of traditional
prosecution and that she wants to divert more arrests to alternatives like the
county’s drug court or a restorative justice program, strategies she says
would reduce recidivism. “If we're prosecuting everything … we've just
essentially created a revolving door of crime,” she told _Bolts_.

Still, Tarkenton says her changes would focus on diverting low-level
misdemeanor cases, despite the repeated reports flagging the county’s approach
to charge a high share of cases as felonies; she does not back a [common
reform](https://boltsmag.org/norfolk-virginia-reelects-reform-prosecutor-
ramin-fatehi-capping-years-of-heated-debate/) among progressive DAs to reduce
how some cases are charged to avoid felony prosecution. On other issues,
Tarkenton said she would support [proposed
legislation](https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-news/politics/15000-people-
in-wa-prisons-cant-vote-a-new-bill-aims-to-change-that/) to entirely abolish
felony disenfranchisement.

### **Wisconsin | Sauk County and Winnebago County sheriffs**

Two Wisconsin counties where GOP sheriffs joined ICE’s 287(g) program feature
contested sheriff elections this fall. Sauk and Winnebago counties are both
politically competitive and could see a partisan flip in November—and in both
the GOP incumbent is retiring.

The Democrats running for sheriff both told _Bolts_ that they would terminate
their counties’ existing 287(g) contracts should they win office.

“To participate in any capacity with a law-enforcement entity, willing to be
as sloppy and degrading to the job they are and trusted to do is just simply
wrong,” Jason Rippl, Democrats' nominee in Winnebago County, said in an email.
He faces Republican Darrin Rice.

“Our priority must be serving the needs of Sauk County, not doing the bidding
of the federal government,” said Ryan Jesberger, Democrats’ nominee in Sauk
County against Republican Matt Burch. However, Jesberger also said he would
retain a separate contract that allows Sauk County to rent jail space to ICE.

### **  
****Honorable mentions**

In Wisconsin’s Racine County, a GOP sheriff is retiring after [targeting
election workers](https://boltsmag.org/trump-aligned-sheriffs-target-election-
officials/) for years as part of investigations into the 2020 election. His
departure guarantees a major changeover, but neither candidate running to
replace him replied to _Bolts_ ’ repeated inquiries into their views.  

In Colorado’s red-leaning El Paso County, Sheriff Joseph Roybal, who [sued
against](https://www.cpr.org/2024/04/11/el-paso-county-sheriff-county-
commissioners-sue-state-of-colorado-over-immigration-laws/) state immigrant
protections, is running for a second term. Candidates with significant
allegations of misconduct are running for sheriff in several counties,
including Kentucky’s [Jefferson County](https://www.courier-
journal.com/story/News/local/public-safety/2026/07/09/bodycam-video-shows-
jefferson-county-sheriff-candidate-incident/90658222007/) (Louisville) and
Oregon’s [Deschutes County](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/07/21/deschutes-
county-sheriff-lt-james-mclaughlin-law-enforcement/).

Texas’ Bexar (San Antonio) and Dallas counties, and Massachusetts’ Bristol
County are sure to have a new prosecutor come 2027, and Maryland’s Baltimore
County is sure to have a new sheriff. The Democratic primary was the key
contest to watch in these blue-leaning counties, though each is still hosting
a general election.

The Democratic primary also settled the prosecutor races in [Burlington,
Vermont](https://boltsmag.org/with-latest-win-progressive-vermont-prosecutor-
looks-to-double-down-on-reforms/), and [Asheville, North
Carolina](https://boltsmag.org/buncombe-county-district-attorney-sheriff-
elections-and-state-preemption/); neither contest even features a Republican
candidate this fall.

Democratic prosecutors in Des Moines, Iowa, and Indianapolis face GOP
challengers who say they’d be more punitive, though it would be a major upset
for either office to flip given that these are blue-leaning jurisdictions.
Similarly, the sheriff of North Carolina’s Buncombe County (Asheville) faces a
GOP challenger in a [context](https://boltsmag.org/buncombe-county-district-
attorney-sheriff-elections-and-state-preemption/) of [recurring
clashes](https://boltsmag.org/north-carolina-ice-and-sheriffs-bill-
immigration/) with the Republican legislature.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2022/06/258768565_237029141830076_4713035306154725487_n.jpg)Kimberly
Graham, the chief prosecutor of Polk County, home to Des Moines, Iowa, is
running for a second term (Kimberly Graham for Polk County Attorney/Facebook)

In Louisiana, Caddo Parish’s Democratic DA was
[once](https://theappeal.org/in-louisiana-a-messenger-of-change-disregards-
his-message/) [heralded as a reformer](https://www.theguardian.com/us-
news/2016/mar/13/caddo-parish-louisiana-death-penalty-capital-district-
attorney) who might bring the death penalty under scrutiny—but he has recently
been [trying to speed up executions](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-limiting-
post-conviction-relief-murrill-landry/). He faces a [GOP
lawmaker](https://john-settle.squarespace.com/settle-talk-
blog/2026/8/19/caddo-da-candidate-vows-aggressive-faster-prosecutions-to-
improve-safety) this fall who supported the [barrage of punitive
laws](https://boltsmag.org/louisiana-special-session-crime-jail-population-
sheriffs/) Louisiana adopted in 2024. In the state’s 15th District (Acadia,
Lafayette, and Vermillion parishes), DA Don Landry is running for reelection
in the wake of a corruption scandal in which a deputy prosecutor was found
guilty of [transforming a local diversion program into a bribery
scheme](https://thecurrentla.com/2025/haynes-guilty-on-all-counts-in-federal-
bribery-trial/).

And the list goes on. _Bolts_ is monitoring __ prosecutor elections in Iowa’s
Dubuque County and Texas’ Hidalgo County, as well as sheriff elections in
Illinois’ Kane and Will counties, New Jersey’s Atlantic County, New Mexico’s
Doña Ana and Sandoval counties, North Carolina’s Nash County, and Utah’s Salt
Lake County.

All this said, hundreds of this year’s [DA and sheriff
races](https://boltsmag.org/criminal-justice-elections-2026-preview/) are
entirely uncontested—in both the primary _and_ the general election.

For instance, plenty of sheriffs who have partnered with ICE are coasting to
reelection with zero opposition, a dynamic that _Bolts_ [has chronicled
](https://boltsmag.org/sheriff-elections-virginia-2025/)in past cycles. This
includes swing counties like Wisconsin’s Brown County and Kenosha County, or
Nevada’s Clark County.

And as _Bolts_ [reported in April](https://boltsmag.org/oregon-uncontested-da-
elections/), not a single one of Oregon’s DA races drew multiple contenders.
Said John Hummel, a former DA in Oregon, “Too rarely does a community have a
conversation about what they want their criminal justice system to be.”
